file: papers/pdf/Merton and Barber - 2004 - A Note on Serendipity in the Humanities.pdf
about: A chapter by Merton and Barber surveying how humanists (collectors, literary scholars, essayists) have interpreted serendipity: as innate trait or gift, as inexplicable faculty, as luck versus merit and hard work, and as a general outlook on life.

candidates.label: Looking for one thing, finding another
candidates.definition: Serendipity is defined as the faculty of making happy accidental discoveries while searching for something else.
candidates.applies_when: The account describes setting out to find or do one thing and instead coming upon something valuable that was not sought.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person found exactly what they were looking for. That is a different kind of happy accident, coded separately as unexpectedly locating a sought item.

candidates.label: Unexpectedly locating a desired item
candidates.definition: A frequent kind of happy accident among collectors is unexpectedly finding a desired item, or recognizing a valuable item before others do.
candidates.applies_when: The person reports stumbling on something they already wanted, or spotting value that others had missed.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The thing found was not sought at all. That fits the 'looking for one thing, finding another' code.

candidates.label: Serendipity as innate gift or trait
candidates.definition: Discoveries are narrated as the product of a natural personal quality, gift or 'cleverness', comparable to perfect pitch. This framing obscures the person's appreciation of the significance of what they found.
candidates.applies_when: The person explains a lucky find by saying they have a knack, gift or natural talent for such finds.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person attributes the find to preparation, effort or skill.

candidates.label: Serendipity as inexplicable sixth sense
candidates.definition: Serendipity is narrated as a mysterious, extrasensory 'radar', clairvoyance or premonition that cannot be explained. The authors note that people tend to dress up discoveries and forget the misses.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes an uncanny instinct or sixth sense that led them to an opportunity, and presents it as unexplainable.

candidates.label: Prepared knowledge of where to look
candidates.definition: Making accidental discoveries requires preparation: knowing in a general way where to look and what to look for. This preparedness is less visible when the knowledge is unsystematic.
candidates.applies_when: The account shows that prior domain knowledge or experience let the person recognize or seek out the unexpected find.

candidates.label: Drama or fun conceals effort
candidates.definition: The human drama of a lucky find, or the enjoyment of browsing, can hide the knowledge, skill and effort the discovery actually required.
candidates.applies_when: The narrative emphasizes the excitement or luck of a find while downplaying, or later revealing, the work and expertise behind it.

candidates.label: Persistence and merit over luck
candidates.definition: Success is explained mainly by persistence, detective skill, scholarship, a network of friendships and fervor, rather than by luck or serendipity.
candidates.applies_when: The person or the narrator attributes the outcome primarily to persistence, skill or relationships, with luck playing a minor part.

candidates.label: Curiosity and open mind
candidates.definition: Minds free of prejudice and driven by lively curiosity, spontaneity, imagination and a sense of adventure are more likely to make unexpected discoveries.
candidates.applies_when: The account credits curiosity, openness or adventurousness with leading the person to an unexpected opportunity.

candidates.label: Routine and conventionality inhibit
candidates.definition: Routine, rigid method and timid, conventional work in a rut suppress serendipity.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes how routine, rigid procedures or a conventional setting kept them from noticing or pursuing unexpected opportunities.

candidates.label: Hard work and active search
candidates.definition: Serendipity requires travel and labor: one must go out, look about and dig. Good luck does not come without hard work.
candidates.applies_when: The account links a lucky break to extensive active searching, travel or effort that put the person where it happened.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The find came while the person was passive. That fits the inexplicable-gift accounts rather than this code.

candidates.label: Selecting among many clues
candidates.definition: Searchers face many promising clues and must select which ones to follow. That selection is made uncertainly, and the excitement comes when a guess proves right.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes choosing which of several leads to pursue, under uncertainty, and following a trail that turned out well.

candidates.label: Pure chance and coincidence
candidates.definition: Chance and unknown causes govern much of life, and people's successes are in large part due to them. People resist admitting this because of vanity or an illusion of control.
candidates.applies_when: The person attributes outcomes to chance or coincidence beyond their control, or the account reveals reluctance to credit chance for success.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Chance combined with the person's recognition or effort fits the definition and mechanism codes.

candidates.label: Serendipitous mindset reframing difficulties
candidates.definition: A 'serendipitaceous' mind, prepared for the worst yet optimistic, finds that obstacles are less formidable than feared. Experience then appears as a series of happy accidents, which helps the person overcome difficulties.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes approaching setbacks expecting the worst but finding that problems turned into opportunities or were not the obstacles they had seemed.
